title: Slice-based latency budgets and kernel degradation playbook for quantized paths
body:
Purpose:
This is a working playbook for how we define, measure, and act on latency budget slices for quantized execution paths (INT8/FP8/GPTQ/AWQ) and how kernel degradation/fallbacks should be governed by telemetry. Unlike kernel ABI or operator contract docs, this focuses on observability-driven decision boundaries and the operational checklist for rollout and incident triage.

Scope and assumptions:
- Applies to serving-runtime lanes that may select mixed-precision kernels or fallback to reference kernels at inference time.
- Covers interactions with KV cache (cold/hot prefixes) and scheduling (batcher/priority preemption).
- Assumes models with typical sequence-length distributions: 8/32/128 tokens slices (we call these S, M, L slices).
- Not a kernel implementation spec; instead a runtime instrumentation and policy playbook to keep SLOs predictable when using low-bit kernels.

High-level goals:
- Define per-slice latency budgets and degradation thresholds for switching kernel families (e.g., INT8 -> INT8-slow -> FP16).
- Ensure fallback triggers are observable, debuggable, and reversible without warm restarts.
- Provide sampling guidelines for synthetic workload calibration and in-production telemetry checks.
- Outline alerting rules and a postmortem checklist specific to quant-path regressions.

Definitions (working):
- slice: a bucketed request shape defined by model, prompt, and expected output length. Current buckets: S (<=16 tokens total), M (17-64), L (65-256).
- latency budget: P99 goal per slice (ms). Budgets below are suggested starting points for internal SLAs.
- baseline kernel: preferred quant kernel (e.g., AWQ-int8-cuda-opt).
- fallback kernel: more conservative kernel (e.g., int8-reference, fp16) used when baseline doesn't meet constraints.
- degradation event: when fallback is used for >= X% of requests in a 5m window for a slice.

Suggested slice budgets (internal starting values):
- S: P99 <= 30ms (target), P99 alert if > 45ms
- M: P99 <= 70ms, alert if > 120ms
- L: P99 <= 220ms, alert if > 350ms
Rationale: small requests must be low-latency for interactive products; larger slices tolerate more batching and cost. Tune per-model.

Quant-path tolerance and fallback policy (telemetry-driven):
1) Continuous profiling: runtime emits profile samples of token-advance time, kv-lookup time, kernel-exec time, dequant/quant overhead, and memory-copy stalls. Sample rate: 1 in 200 requests by default; increase in canaries.
2) Local window checks: for each slice, maintain rolling 1m and 5m P95/P99 for kernel-exec and end-to-end.
3) Soft degrade: if kernel-exec P99 > budget*1.4 for 1m, mark kernel as 'degraded' but continue serving and increase sampling to 1:20. Emit telemetry event: QUANT_KERNEL_DEGRADED {model, slice, kernel, p99_seen}.
4) Hard fallback: if degraded persists for 5m and degrades > 50% of requests in the 5m window, auto-fallback to fallback kernel for that model+slice route. Emit event: QUANT_AUTO_FALLBACK {reason, previous_kernel, new_kernel, diag_id}.
5) Auto-recovery: after fallback, continue sampling. If baseline kernel P99 returns under budget for 10m, auto-reinstate with canary traffic (5% for 10m).
6) Manual override: operators can pin kernel in console with immediate effect and an annotation.

KV cache interactions (special cases):
- Cold prefix penalty: first requests after a new session or after token-shift should be classified as 'cold' and have higher variance. For cold samples we use increased thresholds: allow up to +40% P99 before triggering degrade. Telemetry must attach 'kv_hit_ratio' to QUANT events.
- Hot-prefix optimization: if kv_hit_ratio > 85% for slice S, preemptively allow more aggressive quant kernels (lower guard bands).
- Sharded KV edge case: when KV shards are being rebalanced, expect transient +50% latency; suppress auto-fallbacks during known rebalances (cluster state flag) and raise operational alert instead.

Scheduling interactions and batcher knobs:
- Batcher should publish 'batch-size distribution' per slice and model. High variance can cause kernel-exec P99 spikes.
- If batcher burstiness is root-cause, prefer adjusting batcher-capacity or max-batch-delay before kernel fallback. Auto-fallback should only be used if batcher-config fixes are not available.
- Priority preemption: real-time lanes (low latency slices) get preemption rights; document the preemption metrics correlated with quant degradation.

Telemetry events to emit (minimal):
- QUANT_KERNEL_PROFILE: {model, slice, kernel_family, kernel_name, exec_ms, kv_hit_ratio, gpu_util_pct, queue_ms}
- QUANT_KERNEL_DEGRADED: {model, slice, kernel, p95, p99, sample_count, window}
- QUANT_AUTO_FALLBACK: {model, slice, from_kernel, to_kernel, reason_code, diag_id}
- QUANT_CANARY_REINSTATE: {model, slice, canary_fraction, duration}
- QUANT_KV_TAG: {diag_id, kv_hit_ratio, kv_shard_id, cold_prefix_bool}
- QUANT_SCHED_IMPACT: {model, slice, batcher_size_p95, preemptions}

Instrument fields must be consistent with observability schema (trace_id, request_id, diag_id, monotonic_ts). Telemetry must be linkable to traces for example sessions.

Alerting rules (starter set):
- Alert A1: QUANT_KERNEL_DEGRADED rate > 5 events per minute for same model+slice across any region -> P1 (investigate kernel regressions / rollouts).
- Alert A2: QUANT_AUTO_FALLBACK occurred > 3 times in 1h for a model -> P2 (investigate model-shape or infra stress).
- Alert A3: model-specific P99 (slice S) deviates > 2x baseline for 10m -> P1 (possible infra or scheduling incident).
- Alert A4: kv_hit_ratio drop below 50% for heavy L slices -> P2 (data issue or session churn).

Synthetic calibration harness (how to test before rollout):
- Create per-model workloads that cover S/M/L slices with KV hit ratios at 0%, 50%, 90%.
- Measure kernel-exec P50/P95/P99 for baseline kernels and fallback kernels (report as CSV).
- Run stress scenarios: concurrent small-request bursts, long sequences (L), and rapid new-session churn (cold prefixes).
- Run with disabled batching to capture per-token kernel behavior.

Release and canary playbook (short):
- Stage 0: internal perf lab run against representative hardware (collect full telemetry).
- Stage 1: regional canary (1% traffic) for 24h with sampling ratio 1:10 and elevated logging.
- Stage 2: progressive ramp: 1% -> 5% -> 20% over 48h monitoring QUANT_* events and P99s.
- Stop criteria: any A1 or >20% increase in customer-side errors correlated with fallback.

Debugging and postmortem checklist (when quant regressions found):
- Collect diag_id and trace for representative requests (include QUANT_KERNEL_PROFILE).
- Check batcher distribution and KV hit ratio at times of spikes.
- Verify GPU memory pressure and kernel launch failures.
- Review recent kernel builds and kernel ABI changes (GH PR).
- Determine if blob (weights) changes (quant config) were rolled out.
- If fallback occurred, capture warmup behavior and reinstatement attempt logs.

Open questions / TODOs (short list):
- Fine-tune slice thresholds per model family (LLM vs instruction-tuned). Need dataset of 20 customer models to calibrate. (Action: Priya to run calibration harness Q1 2025).
- Add metric for quant-accuracy drift (QA-side): connect eval-run quality regression to fallback triggers to avoid over-relying on latency-only signals.
- How aggressive should auto-reinstate be in presence of noisy KV caches? Consider requiring sustained under-threshold for 20m for L slices.
- Define operator UX in console for annotating and forcing reinstate with audit logs.

Appendix: example CSV output from calibration harness (column headers):
model, slice, kernel, kv_hit_ratio, sample_count, p50_exec_ms, p95_exec_ms, p99_exec_ms, gpu_util_avg, notes
rw-instruct-13b, S, awq-int8, 90, 10000, 1.9, 5.2, 9.8, 12, 'good'
rw-instruct-13b, M, awq-int8, 30, 8000, 6.1, 18.2, 38.6, 45, 'batch-sensitivity'
rw-instruct-13b, L, gptq-int8, 85, 2000, 22.0, 62.0, 140.2, 78, 'kv-warmed'

Notes on uniqueness: this doc intentionally frames quant-path robustness through the lens of observability, slice-based budgets, and operational automation. It is intended to complement kernel contract specs (see linked GH/JIRA) and to feed concrete telemetry events that kernel engineers and SREs can act on.
